title: Thermal energy transfers
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: B.1#c21 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; B.1#c36 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; B.1#c20 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; B.1#c02 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Specific heat capacity c
items.clue: The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K without a change of phase.

items.label: Apparent brightness b
items.clue: The power of the radiation received from a source per unit area perpendicular to the direction of the radiation, at the observer.

items.label: Evaporation
items.clue: The change from liquid to gas that takes place only at the surface of a liquid, at any temperature, not only at the boiling point.

items.label: Solid (molecular model)
items.clue: Particles are closely packed, held by strong intermolecular forces in fixed mean positions, often in a regular arrangement, and vibrate about those positions.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes evaporation from boiling for water at atmospheric pressure?

options.text: Evaporation occurs only at the boiling point, and only at the surface; boiling occurs throughout the whole liquid.
Evaporation occurs only at the surface and at any temperature; boiling occurs throughout, at the boiling point.
Boiling produces bubbles of air or of hydrogen and oxygen; evaporation produces water vapour.
Boiling occurs throughout while the temperature keeps rising; evaporation occurs at the surface.

questions.explanation: Surface molecules with enough kinetic energy escape at any temperature, which is evaporation. Boiling happens once the liquid reaches its boiling point (100 °C at atmospheric pressure), with vapour forming in bubbles throughout the liquid.

questions.stem: An electric kettle heats 250 g of water from 18 °C to 90 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. How much energy is transferred to the water? Ignore energy transferred to the kettle and surroundings.
questions.explanation: Convert the mass first: m = 250 g = 0.250 kg. Q = mcΔT = 0.250 × 4.18 × 10³ × (90 − 18) = 0.250 × 4180 × 72 = 7.5 × 10⁴ J. A temperature change of 72 °C is 72 K.

questions.stem: Which statement about the mechanisms of thermal energy transfer is correct?

options.text: All three are directed upwards, because heat naturally rises from warm places.
Convection can occur in solids as well as in liquids and gases, just like conduction.
Thermal radiation is emitted only by very hot objects, such as the Sun or a fire.
Only thermal radiation can cross a vacuum; conduction and convection both need a medium.

questions.explanation: Conduction passes energy between particles and convection moves the fluid itself, so both need matter. Thermal radiation is electromagnetic waves, which cross empty space; this is how energy reaches the Earth from the Sun.

questions.stem: One end of a glass rod is held in a flame. How does the molecular model explain conduction of energy along the rod?

options.text: Hot particles travel along the rod from the hot end to the cold end, carrying their energy with them.
Faster-vibrating particles at the hot end pass kinetic energy to their slower neighbours, and so on along the rod.
Heat flows along the rod like a fluid, filling the spaces between the particles as it goes.
Particles at the hot end expand and push against their neighbours, passing the heat along.

questions.explanation: Particles at the hot end have a greater average kinetic energy. Through collisions and the forces between neighbours they pass energy to particles with less, and the energy spreads towards the cold end while the particles stay in place.

questions.stem: A copper rod of length 0.50 m and diameter 2.0 cm is lagged along its sides. One end is kept at 100 °C and the other at 20 °C. The thermal conductivity of copper is 390 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the rate of thermal energy transfer along the rod in steady state?
questions.explanation: r = 1.0 cm = 0.010 m, so A = π(0.010)² = 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ m². |ΔT/Δx| = 80 K/0.50 m = 160 K m⁻¹. Rate = kA|ΔT/Δx| = 390 × 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ × 160 = 19.6 W ≈ 2.0 × 10¹ W, from the hot end to the cold end.

questions.stem: Warm air rises above a radiator in a cold room. Which is the correct explanation?

options.text: Heat naturally rises, so the thermal energy from the radiator moves upwards and carries the air along with it.
Each air molecule expands when it is heated, so it becomes lighter than a cold molecule and floats upwards.
Warm air has almost no weight, unlike the colder air around it, so nothing holds it down and it simply floats upwards.
Air heated by the radiator expands, so it is less dense than the cooler air around it, which sinks and pushes it up.

questions.explanation: Warmed air expands, so a given volume has less mass: its density falls. The denser, cooler air around it sinks beneath it and pushes it upwards, and a convection current forms.

questions.stem: A small metal sphere of radius 5.0 cm is heated to 527 °C. Treat it as a black body and take σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. What power does the sphere emit as thermal radiation?
Two stars appear equally bright when viewed from the Earth. Which statement must be true?

options.text: Equal power per unit area reaches Earth from each.
Each star radiates the same total power out into space.
The two stars are at the same distance from the Earth.
The two stars must have equal surface temperatures.

questions.explanation: Apparent brightness is the power received per unit area at the observer. Equal apparent brightness means exactly this, and nothing more about the stars themselves.

questions.stem: A star has a luminosity of 40 L⊙ and is 25 ly from the Earth. Take L⊙ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W and 1 ly = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. What is the apparent brightness of the star at the Earth?

options.text: 2.0 × 10²⁴ W m⁻²

questions.stem: A surface at 27 °C can be modelled as a black body. Wien's displacement law: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K. At what wavelength is its emission most intense?

options.text: 1.1 × 10⁻⁴ m, in the far infrared
8.7 × 10⁻¹ m, in the radio band
3.6 × 10⁻¹³ m, in the gamma-ray band
9.7 × 10⁻⁶ m, in the infrared

questions.explanation: T = 27 + 273 = 300 K; λ_max = 2.9 × 10⁻³/300 = 9.7 × 10⁻⁶ m (about 10 μm), in the infrared. Everyday objects emit mainly infrared, which is why they do not glow visibly.

questions.stem: A solid is heated by a heater of constant power. Its temperature rises steadily to 80 °C, stays at 80 °C for 5 minutes while the solid melts, and then rises again. Which statement about the 5 minutes at 80 °C is correct?

options.text: Energy is absorbed and makes the molecules move faster, although the temperature reading does not change.
No energy is absorbed by the substance, because its temperature is not changing during this time.
Energy is released as bonds between molecules break, so the intermolecular potential energy decreases.
Energy is absorbed and increases the intermolecular potential energy; the average kinetic energy is constant.

questions.stem: 0.40 kg of ice at 0 °C is melted and the water is then warmed to 20 °C. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; specific latent heat of vaporization of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the total energy that must be supplied?
